title: Plot and interpret
goal: Select a plot that answers a clear question and label its units.
prerequisites: Use summaries, numeric columns, and sorted dates.

cells.title: Compare groups with bars
cells.explanation: A bar chart compares categories. First calculate one statistic per group, then plot those values. The axis label must say whether the height is a mean, count, or total.
cells.code:
df = students()
result = df.groupby("Campus")["Score"].mean().sort_index()
ax = result.plot.bar(color="#28756a", rot=0, figsize=(6, 3.6))
ax.set(title="Mean score by campus (practice data)", xlabel="Campus", ylabel="Mean score (out of 100)", ylim=(0, 100))
plt.tight_layout()
print(result.round(2))
plt.show()

questions.prompt: What does the height of one bar represent?
questions.answer: The mean student Score for that campus in the fictional table.

questions.prompt: Which campus has the higher mean?
questions.answer: RAK, with 81.00, compared with Dubai at about 76.83.

questions.prompt: Does the chart prove campus causes a score difference?
questions.answer: No. These are descriptive summaries from a small fictional dataset, without causal evidence.

cells.task: Plot the number of students in each Program instead, with a count label on the y-axis.
cells.solution:
df = students()
result = df.groupby("Program").size()
ax = result.plot.bar(color="#28756a", rot=0, figsize=(6, 3.6))
ax.set(title="Students by program (practice data)", xlabel="Program", ylabel="Number of students")
ax.set_ylim(bottom=0)
plt.tight_layout()
print(result)
plt.show()
cells.solution_note: Both programs have six students, so their bars have the same height.

options: To identify the statistic and units
check.feedback: A viewer needs to know what each plotted quantity means.

cells.watch: Use a zero baseline for ordinary bar comparisons so bar length remains meaningful.
cells.takeaway: Aggregate first, then label exactly what was plotted.

cells.title: Inspect a distribution
cells.explanation: A histogram counts numeric observations within intervals called bins. It shows the distribution of individual values, rather than a summary for each named category. Bin choices can change the visual impression.
cells.code:
df = students()
result = pd.cut(df["Score"], bins=[50, 60, 70, 80, 90, 100], right=False).value_counts(sort=False)
ax = df["Score"].plot.hist(bins=[50, 60, 70, 80, 90, 100], color="#28756a", edgecolor="white", figsize=(6, 3.6))
ax.set(title="Distribution of scores (practice data)", xlabel="Score (out of 100)", ylabel="Number of students")
plt.tight_layout()
print(result)
plt.show()

questions.prompt: What is counted along the vertical axis?
questions.answer: Students whose scores fall inside each interval.

questions.prompt: How is this different from a bar chart of campus means?
questions.answer: A histogram groups numeric values into intervals; campus bars compare named groups.

cells.task: Use wider bins [50, 75, 100] and compare the count table and visual shape.
cells.hint: Change the bin edges in both pd.cut and plot.hist.
cells.solution:
df = students()
result = pd.cut(df["Score"], bins=[50, 75, 100], right=False).value_counts(sort=False)
ax = df["Score"].plot.hist(bins=[50, 75, 100], color="#28756a", edgecolor="white", figsize=(6, 3.6))
ax.set(title="Scores with wider bins (practice data)", xlabel="Score (out of 100)", ylabel="Number of students")
plt.tight_layout()
print(result)
plt.show()
cells.solution_note: The two wider bins contain four scores below 75 and eight scores from 75 up to 100.

check.prompt: What happens when bin widths change?
check.feedback: Binning changes the display, not the underlying observations.

cells.watch: Histogram libraries usually include the upper endpoint of the last bin; pd.cut(right=False) does not. These sample scores contain no endpoint value of 100.
cells.takeaway: Check bin boundaries when interpreting distributions.

cells.title: Compare two measurements
cells.explanation: A scatter plot places one point at each pair of numeric measurements. This can reveal a pattern, an unusual observation, or a gap. Correlation describes association; it does not establish why the pattern occurs.
cells.code:
df = students()
result = df[["Study_Hours", "Score"]].corr().loc["Study_Hours", "Score"]
ax = df.plot.scatter(x="Study_Hours", y="Score", color="#28756a", figsize=(6, 3.6))
ax.set(title="Study time and score (practice data)", xlabel="Study hours per week", ylabel="Score (out of 100)")
plt.tight_layout()
print("Pearson correlation:", round(result, 3))
plt.show()

questions.answer: One student with a Study_Hours value and a Score value.

questions.prompt: Will the overall pattern slope upward or downward?
questions.answer: Upward in this fictional table: higher study hours generally accompany higher scores.

questions.prompt: Can this prove that adding one hour causes a fixed score increase?
questions.answer: No. The table is fictional and descriptive, and the plot does not control other factors.

cells.task: Plot Attendance against Score and calculate their Pearson correlation.
cells.hint: Replace Study_Hours with Attendance in both the correlation and plot.
cells.solution:
df = students()
result = df[["Attendance", "Score"]].corr().loc["Attendance", "Score"]
ax = df.plot.scatter(x="Attendance", y="Score", color="#28756a", figsize=(6, 3.6))
ax.set(title="Attendance and score (practice data)", xlabel="Attendance (%)", ylabel="Score (out of 100)")
plt.tight_layout()
print("Pearson correlation:", round(result, 3))
plt.show()
cells.solution_note: The revised plot compares attendance percentages with scores. Its association still does not establish causation.

check.prompt: What does a positive correlation indicate?
options: One variable must cause the other
Every point lies on a straight line
check.feedback: A positive correlation describes the direction of association, not a causal mechanism.

cells.watch: Outliers, restricted ranges, and missing data can affect correlation; inspect the actual points.
cells.takeaway: Use scatter plots to inspect relationships without claiming causes.

cells.title: Show change over time
cells.explanation: A line chart uses an ordered horizontal axis to show change. Reindexing to a daily grid keeps the missing date visible as a gap. A line across an unobserved day can otherwise suggest continuity that was not measured.
cells.code:
df = attendance()
df["Date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["Date"], format="%Y-%m-%d")
result = df.set_index("Date")["Visitors"].sort_index().asfreq("D")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.6))
ax.plot(result.index, result, marker="o", color="#28756a")
ax.set(title="Daily visitors (practice data)", xlabel="Date", ylabel="Recorded visitors")
ax.set_ylim(bottom=0)
fig.autofmt_xdate()
plt.tight_layout()
print(result)
plt.show()

questions.answer: It gives the horizontal axis chronological meaning and supports a regular daily index.
October 4, whose visitor count is missing.

questions.prompt: Does the gap mean no visitors came?
questions.answer: No. The count is unknown for that day.

cells.task: Store the daily counts in daily and the three-day rolling mean in result, requiring three known daily values. Plot daily and result together with labels for both lines.
cells.hint: Calculate result from daily.rolling(3, min_periods=3).mean(), then plot both Series on the same axes.
cells.solution:
df = attendance()
df["Date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["Date"], format="%Y-%m-%d")
daily = df.set_index("Date")["Visitors"].sort_index().asfreq("D")
result = daily.rolling(3, min_periods=3).mean()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.6))
ax.plot(daily.index, daily, marker="o", label="Daily count", color="#28756a")
ax.plot(result.index, result, marker="s", label="3-day mean", color="#9c6b28")
ax.set(title="Daily visitors and rolling mean (practice data)", xlabel="Date", ylabel="Visitors")
ax.set_ylim(bottom=0)
ax.legend()
fig.autofmt_xdate()
plt.tight_layout()
print(result.round(2))
plt.show()
cells.solution_note: The rolling mean is available only on October 3 and October 7 because other windows lack three known values.

check.prompt: Why leave a visible gap for the missing day?
options: It proves the count was zero
check.feedback: A gap prevents an unknown value from being mistaken for an observed zero.

cells.watch: A smooth line does not create new observations; report how any smoothing was calculated.
cells.takeaway: Time order, gaps, and transformations belong in the explanation.
